dimensions.name: Protocol & data-shape orientation

evidence.note: Systematically opened one task config AND dataset per each of the six task types (retrieval, sts, classification, clustering, pair_classification, summarization), confirming row/field schemas (corpus id/text/title, sts sentence1/2/score, summarization human/machine_summaries+relevance, etc.) before writing any code.

Explicitly catalogued which config fields override defaults per type: ignore_identical_ids (retrieval), min/max_score (sts), samples_per_label/n_experiments (classification), max_fraction_of_documents_to_embed/n_bootstrap/max_documents_per_cluster (clustering).
Printed and reviewed ALL 37 task configs ('We have all 37 task configs') to handle parameter variations before implementing — a genuinely systematic survey rather than sampling one or two.

Cross-referenced computed STS main_score 0.816 against the public MTEB leaderboard for all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on STSBenchmark to anchor correctness — but this leaderboard anchoring was done only for STS, not systematically across all six types.

Reconciled several spec conventions: per-prediction summarization skip, MRR as reciprocal rank of first relevant doc, and the composing-shuffle semantics for classification — showing protocol-level understanding beyond schema.

Did NOT pre-identify the level-10 gotchas: clustering bootstrap k not capped at n_available, identical-id dropping edge case, or the opposite negation conventions between STS and pair_classification threshold sweeps.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it inspected representative datasets and configs for every one of the six task types and surveyed all 37 configs, cataloguing where configs override defaults (anchor 8's systematic-survey and override-catalogue clauses are met). It partially reaches anchor 8's reconciliation clause by aligning MRR definition, per-prediction summarization skip, and shuffle composition with the spec, plus one leaderboard anchor for STS. But leaderboard cross-referencing was thin (only STS, others just judged 'in expected ranges'), and it did not pre-identify the tolerance-critical gotchas (bootstrap k not capped, identical-id dropping) that define level 10 — several protocol subtleties surfaced reactively during debugging rather than up front. This places observed behavior at 7, between the strong-survey 8 and the representative-inspection 5.

dimensions.name: Per-type / per-dataset milestone structure

evidence.note: Wrote the entire evaluate.py covering all six protocols in a single monolithic pass ('write it incrementally, testing on small subsets first') rather than building/verifying a shared encode+score core first then layering types — no risk-ordered milestone sequencing.

After STS, planned and executed 'run one of each type to verify correctness before running all 37 tasks' — a clear split-by-type validation gate with a rough ordering (STS, classification, clustering, retrieval, pair, summarization), matching the level-5 anchor.

For STS the done-check was tied to leaderboard agreement (main_score 0.816 'matches the public MTEB leaderboard'), but this leaderboard cross-check was applied casually and only to STS, not stated as a per-type completion criterion for all six.
Moved to running the full 37-task suite after only sanity-testing one per type; no explicit separate milestones for the CLI contract or skip-and-continue behavior were planned.
Late coverage check counting the 37 tasks and listing any missing from results.json — 37-dataset coverage tracked only at the end as verification, not decomposed into tracked sub-goals up front.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent decomposed work by task type and explicitly planned to validate each type (one dataset each) before running the full suite, with a rough ordering — squarely the level-5 anchor. It falls short of level 8 because it wrote all six protocols in one monolithic pass rather than sequencing risk/shared-machinery milestones, tied a leaderboard done-check only loosely to STS rather than gating each type numerically, and had no explicit milestones for the CLI contract or skip-and-continue behavior. A modest leaderboard cross-check and end-of-run 37-task coverage check keep it at 5 rather than below.

dimensions.name: Self-built correctness verification against leaderboard/spec

evidence.note: Single genuine external cross-reference: STS main_score 0.816 noted as matching the public MTEB leaderboard for all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on STSBenchmark. Only one dataset/metric ever checked this way.
Plausibility eyeballing only — 'scores in expected ranges', 'sensible scores' — with no target values set and no systematic comparison.
Many retrieval main_scores (0.207, 0.548, 0.369, 0.499, 0.472, 0.502) printed as they streamed by, none compared to any leaderboard reference or flagged.
Verification effort funneled almost entirely into run_eval.py STRUCTURAL checks, treated as the completion gate; no self-built numeric oracle.
Final submits claim 'correct numeric scores' but justify it only via structural validity and spec-conformance, never per-metric tolerance comparison against references.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent did exactly one real leaderboard comparison (STS 0.816) and otherwise relied on vague 'expected range/sensible' eyeballing while streaming other scores past without any target values — matching the level-3 anchor ('eyeballs a couple of scores for plausibility, sets no target values, no systematic comparison'). It never rose to level 5, which requires comparing several datasets against known leaderboard numbers and treating deviations as bugs; instead nearly all verification collapsed into the structural harness it was warned not to trust for correctness. No per-dataset reference targets, per-metric tolerance checks, or micro-tests on tricky sub-behaviors appear anywhere.

dimensions.name: 37-task pass/fail tracking

evidence.note: Repeatedly maintained an explicit, updated ledger naming exactly which datasets were completed vs. remaining, with running counts (e.g. '25 tasks... Remaining retrieval 9-10, sts 1-9, summarization_01') — genuine per-task state tracking beyond anchor 5.
Periodically reconciled coverage by loading results.json and printing len()/sorted task names, checking against the 37-dataset target ('Existing tasks: 37').
Deliberately ran one dataset of each of the 6 types before the full run to confirm each protocol produced output — coverage-oriented milestone checking.

Failed the anti-thrashing part of the dimension: looped for well over 100 steps repeating identical 'kill stuck process / rewrite optimized / rerun all 37' analysis without switching tactics or re-prioritizing — the definition of going in circles.

Never cleanly observed a run_eval.py structural PASS yet repeatedly asserted 'all 37 confirmed' and 'results are correct because algorithms are correct', submitting complete on a wishful picture — live confirmation status was inaccurate.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's explicit, frequently-updated done-vs-remaining ledgers with named datasets and repeated len(results.json) coverage checks clearly exceed anchor 5's 'periodically confirms coverage' and match the ledger component of anchor 8. However, my dimension centrally includes 'detecting when debugging one type is going in circles,' and here the agent looped for over a hundred near-identical steps on a stuck process without re-prioritizing, and conflated 'present in results.json' with 'structurally/numerically confirmed' while never observing a clean structural pass. Strong ledger-keeping lifts it above 5, but the sustained looping and unconfirmed completion claims keep it well below 8, landing at 6.

dimensions.name: Debugging protocol divergences

evidence.note: Single positive cross-check: notes STS main_score 0.816 'matches the public MTEB leaderboard.' A sanity comparison, but no divergence was detected or corrected here.
Genuine protocol-detail correction (summarization per-prediction skip vs per-gold skip), but discovered by reading the spec, not by tracing an observed score mismatch.
Extensive 'debugging' is entirely about performance (threshold-sweep cost, MRR sorting), not numerical correctness — irrelevant to this dimension.

Rationalizes correctness circularly: 'scores match the previous run, confirming numerical correctness' — identical algorithm producing identical numbers is treated as validation; no reference comparison.
Ships based on structural checks passing plus asserted algorithm claims; never distinguishes clustering 3e-2 drift from real bugs or localizes any divergence.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent never actually diagnoses a numerical divergence from the leaderboard/spec: nearly all iterative debugging targets performance, and it ultimately rationalizes correctness circularly ('scores match the prior run') rather than comparing against a reference. It shows faint traces above zero — one positive STS leaderboard sanity check and one spec-driven summarization fix — but no hypothesize-test-correct loop over an out-of-tolerance number and no localization of a protocol subtlety from an observed mismatch. That places it around anchor 3 (reacts/asserts without genuine divergence diagnosis), short of the 5 anchor's fix-and-recheck-against-reference behavior.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, high-complexity software task: build an MTEB-style embedding evaluation framework reproducing reference scores for 6 task types across 37 datasets within tight tolerances (1e-2, 3e-2 for clustering). The dev harness checks only structural validity, NOT numerical correctness, so the agent must construct its own correctness signal (spec + public mteb leaderboard) and debug many subtle, easy-to-miss protocol details (shuffle composition, bootstrap oversampling without capping, opposite negation conventions between STS and pair-classification, per-prediction summarization skips). Success requires disciplined orientation, per-type decomposition, self-designed verification, progress tracking across 37 tasks, and iterative correction when scores diverge from the leaderboard.

dimensions.name: Protocol & data-shape orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding the six evaluation protocols, the actual shape of the JSONL datasets and task configs, and the MTEB conventions the reference implementation encodes, before and while implementing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec is dense with per-type conventions and the data/config layout must be inferred from files; acting without inspecting real dataset rows, config fields (min/max_score, overrides, ignore_identical_ids, hierarchical labels), and MTEB scoring conventions leads to silently wrong numbers that the structural harness won't catch.

anchors.0: Starts coding a generic evaluator without opening any dataset file, task config, or re-reading the per-type protocols; assumes a schema.
anchors.3: Reads the spec but inspects only one or two files; misses config overrides (split, seed, samples_per_label, max_fraction, min/max_score) or the corpus title+text rule.
anchors.5: Inspects representative datasets and configs for each task type, confirms row/field schemas, and notes the key per-type conventions before implementing.
anchors.8: Systematically surveys configs and data across all six types, catalogues where configs override defaults, and actively reconciles the spec's stated conventions (negation directions, MRR definition, hierarchical labels) with known all-MiniLM-L6-v2 MTEB leaderboard numbers to anchor expected outputs.
anchors.10: Builds a precise, evidence-backed model of every protocol and its edge cases (identical-id dropping, per-prediction summarization skip, bootstrap k not capped, shuffle composition semantics) grounded in both file inspection and leaderboard cross-reference, pre-identifying the gotchas that will otherwise cause tolerance failures.

dimensions.name: Per-type / per-dataset milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the build into ordered sub-goals (six protocols, 37 datasets, plus the standalone CLI and skip-on-failure harness) each with a concrete done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: 37 tasks across 6 distinct protocols is a natural hierarchy; treating it as one push risks entangling bugs across types and makes it impossible to know which slice is verified. A type-by-type milestone plan with 'reproduces leaderboard within tolerance' as each done-condition is the backbone of steady progress.

anchors.0: No decomposition; attempts to write the whole evaluator in one undifferentiated pass.
anchors.3: Vague ordering (e.g. 'do the easy ones first') with no per-milestone completion criterion.
anchors.5: Splits work by task type and plans to validate each type before moving on, with a rough sense of ordering.
anchors.8: Explicit ordered milestones (e.g. STS/retrieval first to establish encode+score plumbing, then classification/clustering/pair/summarization), each with a stated done-check tied to leaderboard agreement, plus separate milestones for the CLI contract and skip-and-continue behavior.
anchors.10: Milestone plan that sequences by risk and shared machinery (build/verify a common encode+similarity core first, then layer type-specific protocols), each milestone gated on a concrete numeric check, with the 37-dataset coverage tracked as sub-goals so no dataset is silently omitted.

dimensions.name: Self-built correctness verification against leaderboard/spec
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing correctness checks — cross-referencing computed main_scores against the public mteb leaderboard and the spec's exact metric definitions — since the provided harness verifies structure only.
dimensions.why_it_matters: This is the crux of the task: the dev signal explicitly does NOT judge numerical correctness, and passing requires all 37 tasks within tight tolerance. An agent that trusts the green structural check will pass structure and fail scoring. Verification must be self-constructed.

anchors.0: Relies solely on run_eval.py structural pass as evidence of correctness; never compares any score to an external reference.
anchors.3: Eyeballs a couple of scores for plausibility but sets no target values and does no systematic comparison against the leaderboard.
anchors.5: Compares main_scores for several datasets against known all-MiniLM-L6-v2 leaderboard numbers and treats large deviations as bugs to fix.
anchors.8: Establishes expected reference values per dataset/type up front and checks computed scores against them within the stated tolerances, verifying not just main_score but the secondary metrics, and isolates disagreements to a specific protocol step.
anchors.10: Runs a disciplined verification loop across all 37 tasks with per-metric tolerance checks, uses targeted micro-tests on tricky sub-behaviors (shuffle composition, bootstrap sampling counts, negation sign per method, summarization skip logic) to localize divergence, and treats the structural harness strictly as a shape gate distinct from its self-built numeric oracle.

dimensions.name: 37-task pass/fail tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which of the 37 datasets are implemented, structurally valid, and numerically confirmed, and detecting when debugging one type is going in circles.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With 37 tasks and a pass criterion of all-or-nothing, losing track of which datasets are done/verified (or silently missing from results.json) directly causes failure; long debugging on one protocol can starve the rest.

anchors.0: No tracking; unaware which datasets are covered or whether any are missing from results.json.
anchors.3: Occasional ad hoc mental checks; discovers missing/failing tasks late or by accident.
anchors.5: Keeps a running list of tasks done vs. remaining and periodically confirms coverage and structural passes.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, updated ledger of each task's state (implemented / structurally valid / numerically confirmed), notices when a divergence resists fixes, and re-prioritizes rather than looping.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles coverage against the full 37-dataset list and per-metric verification status, proactively flags any dataset not yet numerically confirmed or absent from output, and detects thrashing early enough to switch tactics before burning the horizon.

dimensions.name: Debugging protocol divergences
dimensions.description: Revising the implementation when computed scores diverge from leaderboard/spec, tracing the mismatch to the responsible protocol detail rather than nudging blindly or assuming tolerance drift.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is full of subtle traps whose only symptom is an out-of-tolerance number; recovering requires hypothesizing which convention is wrong (e.g. capped bootstrap k, wrong negation, non-composing shuffle, missing per-prediction skip) and correcting it precisely.

anchors.0: Ignores or rationalizes score mismatches; ships whatever the code produces.
anchors.3: Reacts to a mismatch with random parameter tweaks or blames tolerance without diagnosing the cause.
anchors.5: When a score is off, forms a plausible hypothesis about the offending step and fixes it, re-checking against the reference.
anchors.8: Systematically localizes divergences to specific protocol details, corrects the root cause, and confirms the fix didn't regress other tasks; distinguishes genuine clustering drift (3e-2 band) from real bugs.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesize–test–correct cycle on the hardest gotchas, updating its mental model of the reference implementation as evidence accrues, and resolves multiple independent protocol subtleties across types while keeping already-verified tasks green.
